subtype: Holding arms close to the body [Expressing]
passage: The wedding hall in Amritsar was loud, packed with aunties and drums, and the lights kept flickering. Shankar, five, kept his arms pressed tight to his sides, and stayed half behind his father Lokesh's leg. A relative bent down. "Come, give me a hug!" Shankar leaned away. Lokesh said easily, "He needs a minute, ji. He's warming up." After some time, Shankar was standing at the edge of the dance floor, his arms slowly loosening, watching the dhol player.

qa.q: Where was the wedding held?
qa.a: It was held in a hall in Amritsar.

qa.q: What might Shankar have been feeling with his arms pressed tight to his sides?
qa.a: He was probably cautious and a bit overwhelmed by the noisy crowd of new people. He could also have been just tired.

qa.q: How did Lokesh help Shankar?
qa.a: He stayed close, explained that Shankar needed a minute and didn't push a hug, so Shankar could warm up at his own pace.

qa.q: How might the relative feel when Shankar leans away?
qa.a: They may feel a little rebuffed, but Lokesh's easy words help them see it as shyness and not rudeness.

grounding: A shy child tucks his arms to his body around new people, and time with a familiar adult nearby helps.

subtype: Holding arms close to the body [Expressing]
passage: Pradeep's cousin Siddharth had just moved to Bhopal, and on his first day at the new school, the class teacher led him in. Siddharth, six, kept his arms tucked against his ribs and looked at the floor. "This is Siddharth," said the teacher. The class said, "Hello!" He gave the smallest nod. Pradeep, sitting nearby, saved him a seat and didn't say much. By break time Siddharth was holding a pencil box with both hands, arms a little looser, and asked Pradeep, "Which game do you play?"

qa.q: What did Pradeep do for Siddharth?
qa.a: He saved him a seat and didn't say much.

qa.q: What does Siddharth's tucked arms and lowered gaze suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: They suggest he feels cautious and shy among new people. He could also just be feeling tired from the move.

qa.q: What could the teacher do to help Siddharth settle in?
qa.a: The teacher can let him stay near Pradeep and give him time before asking him to speak or perform.

qa.q: How might Pradeep see Siddharth's behaviour on his first morning?
qa.a: He may see a quiet new boy who needs a friendly face, and he responds by sitting close.

grounding: A shy child keeps his arms tucked around new people, and time with a familiar person helps.

passage:
“Wasim, come say hello to Uncle and Aunty.”
Wasim stood in the doorway of the new neighbours' flat with his arms pressed flat against his sides, hands tucked into his shorts pockets.
“Hello, Wasim!” said the aunty. “Want some juice?”
Wasim looked at Saurabh Chacha's knees and said nothing.
“He takes a little time,” Saurabh said. He crouched. “You can stay next to me. No rush.”
Wasim leaned on his leg. Twenty minutes later one hand came out of a pocket, and he pointed at the juice.

qa.q: Where did Wasim put his hands?
qa.a: He tucked them into his shorts pockets, with his arms pressed flat against his sides.

qa.q: What do Wasim's arms pressed to his sides suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest he felt shy and cautious with new people in a new place. He might also have felt a bit overwhelmed by being greeted so directly.

qa.q: Which choice by Saurabh worked, and why?
qa.a: He let Wasim stay close and said there was no rush, so Wasim could warm up in his own time.

qa.q: How might the new aunty see Wasim's silence?
qa.a: She might wonder if he disliked her, but Saurabh's words help her see he just needs time.

grounding: A shy child keeps his arms tucked to his body around new people, and a familiar adult nearby helps him warm up.

subtype: Holding arms close to the body [Expressing]
passage:
Settling-in note, day one. Written by Bhavna, nursery teacher.
Vidya arrived holding her father's finger. After he left, she stood by the cubbies with her arms folded tight against her chest and her elbows tucked in. When children came near, she pulled her arms in even closer. I didn't make her join. I sat on a low stool close to her and sorted crayons, humming. By snack time she had moved to my side. At going-home time she reached out, took a red crayon, and drew one circle.

qa.q: What colour crayon did Vidya take?
qa.a: A red crayon.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling as she pulled her arms in closer when children came near?
qa.a: She was probably shy and cautious, protecting herself in a new place without her father. She may also have been sad that he had left.

qa.q: What might Bhavna try on day two?
qa.a: Bhavna could sit near Vidya again and offer the crayons early, letting her join at her own pace.

qa.q: How might Vidya's father feel reading this note?
qa.a: He would likely feel reassured that the teacher was patient and that Vidya slowly began to relax.

grounding: The note shows a shy child keeping her arms tucked in around new people, and time and a nearby adult helping.

subtype: Holding arms close to the body [Expressing]
passage: The naming ceremony filled the courtyard with relatives Payal had never met. She stood pressed against Bhavna Maasi, arms tight to her body, hands clasped at her tummy. When a loud uncle bent to pinch her cheek, she tucked her chin and pulled her elbows in. Maasi gently stepped between them. “She's still getting used to everyone.” She let Payal hold the end of her dupatta. By the time the sweets came round, Payal was holding out one hand for a laddoo.

qa.q: What did Bhavna Maasi let Payal hold?
qa.a: The end of her dupatta.

qa.q: Why did Payal pull her elbows in when the uncle bent down?
qa.a: She felt shy and uneasy with a loud stranger reaching for her face, and wanted to keep herself small and safe.

qa.q: What went right in how Maasi handled the uncle?
qa.a: She calmly stepped between them and explained, which protected Payal without making a scene.

qa.q: How might the loud uncle see Payal's pulled-in arms?
qa.a: He might think she is unfriendly, but Maasi's words help him understand she just needs time.

grounding: A shy child keeps her arms close to her body among new relatives, and a familiar aunt nearby helps.

subtype: Holding arms close to the body [Expressing]
passage:
On his first morning at the playgroup in Nairobi, Kaito stood by the door with his arms pressed tight against his sides, hands tucked under his armpits. He watched the other children banging drums but did not move.

Teacher Wanjiru didn't pull him in. She put a small drum near his father's chair and went back to the circle.

Kaito's father sat down. After a while Kaito leaned on his father's knee. Then one hand came out and tapped the drum, very softly.

qa.q: Where did Teacher Wanjiru put the small drum?
qa.a: Near his father's chair.

qa.q: What was Kaito feeling as he stood by the door with his arms pressed to his sides?
qa.a: He was most likely shy and cautious in a new place full of strangers. He might also have been curious, since he kept watching the drums.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Wanjiru gave Kaito time and left the drum near his father instead of pulling him in, so he could join at his own pace with a familiar adult close by.

qa.q: What would change if Wanjiru had pulled Kaito into the circle?
qa.a: He might have become more frightened and kept his arms tucked even tighter, taking longer to feel safe.

grounding: It shows a shy child keeping his arms tucked in around new people and loosening up with time and a familiar adult nearby.
